title: Face-to-face communication: pros & cons
blurb: Know exactly what face-to-face communication does well, where it falls down, and how exam options try to trick you.
question: A project manager must tell a residents' group that building works will overrun by two months and agree new working hours with them. Why is a face-to-face meeting a strong choice, and what must the project manager do afterwards to cover its main weakness?

teach.h: What counts as face to face
teach.body: Face-to-face communication happens in person: the people are physically together at the same time. Think meetings, workshops, one-to-ones, kick-off sessions, site walks and presentations to a room. In plain English: you can see each other's faces, hear each other's tone and respond on the spot. A video call is NOT face to face in this exam; it is virtual.

teach.h: Face to face at a glance

root.label: Face to face
root.sub: In person, same place, same time

teach.caption: The more cues the receiver gets, the easier it is to decode the meaning correctly and spot confusion early.

teach.h: The advantages, and why they matter
teach.body: Face to face gives the fullest picture: words, tone and body language together. Feedback is immediate, so confusion is spotted and cleared up at once. Seeing people in person builds trust and relationships, which is why kick-offs are often held face to face. It is the best choice for sensitive, complex or contentious topics: bad news, negotiation, conflict and difficult decisions.

rows.label: Costly: travel, venues, hours away from work
Hard to arrange across locations and time zones
No automatic record: minutes are needed
Can be dominated by a few loud voices

teach.note: Each of these is a favourite exam answer when the stem asks for a disadvantage of face to face.

teach.h: Scenario: the Northgate Hospital car park
teach.body: Tom manages a car park extension next to a housing estate. The works will overrun by two months and residents are angry about noise. He holds a face-to-face meeting in the community hall: he can read the mood, answer questions straight away and negotiate later start times. Trust improves. But the contractor team is spread across three depots, so their weekly progress meeting is held as a video call instead, and Tom emails the residents' meeting notes the next day.

teach.text: Watch for advantages that belong to OTHER methods. 'Creates a permanent audit trail' is physical (and often virtual), not face to face. 'Cheap and quick to reach a dispersed team' is virtual. And remember: a video call is virtual, even though you can see faces.

teach.h: Getting the best from a face-to-face meeting
teach.caption: Minutes and a follow-up note cover face to face's biggest weakness: no automatic record.

items: Face to face = in person, same place, same time (video calls are virtual).
Advantages: body language and tone, immediate feedback, builds trust, best for sensitive or complex topics and negotiation.
Disadvantages: time-consuming, costly (travel), hard across locations, no automatic record, can be dominated by a few.
Cover the gaps: plan an agenda, chair firmly, take minutes, follow up in writing.

summary: You can now outline the advantages of face-to-face communication (richest cues, immediate feedback, trust, best for sensitive or complex topics) and its disadvantages (time, cost, location, no automatic record, domination by a few). You can also reject options that really describe physical or virtual methods.

A.q: Which of the following is an advantage of face-to-face communication?
options: It creates an automatic written record
Body language and tone can be read
It reaches dispersed teams at low cost
It can be re-read later at any time
A.why: In person, the receiver gets words, tone and body language together, the richest set of cues of any method.

whyNot.0: Face to face leaves no automatic record; someone has to take minutes.
whyNot.2: Gathering a dispersed team in person is costly; low-cost reach is a virtual advantage.
whyNot.3: Being able to re-read a message is an advantage of physical (and written virtual) methods.

A.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of face-to-face communication?
options: It gives no chance of immediate feedback
It cannot convey the speaker's tone
It makes it harder to build relationships
It can be costly and slow to arrange
A.why: Bringing people together takes time and often travel, venues and hours away from other work.

whyNot.0: Immediate feedback is one of face to face's biggest strengths.
whyNot.1: Tone of voice is fully conveyed in person.
whyNot.2: Face to face is the best method for building trust and relationships.

A.q: For which message is face-to-face communication the most suitable?
options: Telling a supplier their contract will end
Issuing the monthly cost report to all staff
Displaying visitor safety rules at the gate
Sharing the dial-in link for a weekly call
A.why: Ending a contract is sensitive and may lead to negotiation. Face to face allows empathy, immediate questions and careful handling of reactions.

whyNot.1: A routine report to many people suits a written or virtual method.
whyNot.2: Standing rules for every visitor suit a physical sign or notice board.
whyNot.3: A link is simple factual information best sent by email or message.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of face-to-face communication?
options: Questions can be answered on the spot
Trust is built more quickly in person
It provides a built-in audit trail
Reactions can be seen as they happen
B.why: Face to face leaves no record unless minutes are taken. An audit trail is an advantage of physical and written virtual methods.

whyNot.0: Immediate questions and answers are a key face-to-face advantage.
whyNot.1: Building trust and relationships is a recognised advantage of meeting in person.
whyNot.3: Seeing reactions (body language) helps the speaker adjust in real time, an advantage.

B.q: In a face-to-face design review, two senior managers talk for most of the session and the junior engineers say nothing. Which disadvantage of face to face does this show?
options: It relies on a stable internet link
A few people can dominate the discussion
Its tone is easily misread in writing
It is slow to print and distribute
B.why: Meetings can be dominated by a few confident or senior voices, so others' views are lost. A firm chair helps prevent this.

whyNot.0: Dependence on technology is a virtual disadvantage.
whyNot.2: Misread tone in writing is a disadvantage of written methods, not of meeting in person.
whyNot.3: Printing and distribution delays are physical disadvantages.

B.q: Why is face-to-face communication well suited to negotiating a revised delivery date with a contractor?
options: Objections can be raised and settled at once
Agreements are recorded without any minutes
It is the cheapest way to involve both parties
It avoids the need for any later confirmation
B.why: Negotiation needs fast back-and-forth. Face to face lets each side raise objections, read reactions and settle points immediately.

whyNot.1: Face to face has no automatic record; minutes are still needed.
whyNot.2: Travel and time often make it the costlier option.
whyNot.3: Agreements should still be confirmed in writing afterwards.

C.q: Which TWO are disadvantages of face-to-face communication? 1) Travel and venue costs. 2) No chance of immediate feedback. 3) No record unless minutes are taken. 4) Reliance on internet access.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Face to face can be costly (travel, venues) and leaves no record unless someone takes minutes.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: immediate feedback is a face-to-face strength.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: feedback is immediate, and meeting in person does not need the internet.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: reliance on the internet is a virtual disadvantage.

C.q: A project team works from Leeds, Pune and Toronto. The sponsor insists every weekly update is held face to face. Which disadvantage is most exposed?
options: Updates would have no non-verbal cues
Updates would depend on a stable network
It is hard to arrange across locations
Updates would be slow to print and post
C.why: Gathering people from three continents every week is impractical: time zones, travel time and cost all count against face to face.

whyNot.0: Face to face gives the fullest non-verbal cues; a lack of them is a virtual drawback.
whyNot.1: Network dependence is a virtual disadvantage.
whyNot.3: Printing and posting delays are physical disadvantages.

C.q: A face-to-face workshop agrees three changes to scope. What should the project manager do next to offset the main weakness of the method?
options: Hold a second workshop to repeat the points
Issue minutes recording the agreed changes
Ask the sponsor to verbally restate the changes
Leave it, as all attendees heard the decisions
C.why: Face to face has no automatic record, so decisions can later be disputed. Minutes (then formal change control) create the record.

whyNot.0: Another meeting adds cost and still leaves no written record.
whyNot.2: A verbal restatement is still unrecorded.
whyNot.3: Memories differ over time; without a record the decisions may be disputed.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding with the venue
reteach.question: You could plan your wedding with the venue by email, or sit down with the coordinator in person. What does the in-person meeting give you, and what does it cost?

blocks.body: In the meeting you see the coordinator wince when you mention 200 guests, so you ask about the room limit at once. You negotiate the menu price there and then, and you leave trusting them. But it took a half-day off work and a long drive, your partner couldn't make it, and a week later nobody can remember whether the late bar was agreed. That is face to face: rich and personal, but costly and unrecorded.

blocks.text: The fix is the same as on a project: send a short note after the meeting confirming what was agreed. Face to face for the conversation, writing for the record.

explain.h: What is, and is not, face to face
explain.body: Face to face means physically together: meetings, workshops, one-to-ones, site walks, presentations. A video call or phone call is virtual. A printed report is physical. The exam can test this boundary.

test.q: Which of the following is an example of face-to-face communication?
options: A cameras-on video call with the client
A one-to-one meeting in the site office
A printed newsletter handed to each worker
A phone call with the project sponsor
test.why: A one-to-one in the site office has both people physically present at the same time.

whyNot.0: Seeing faces on a screen is still virtual communication.
whyNot.2: A newsletter handed out is physical communication, even if delivered by hand.
whyNot.3: A phone call is a virtual method.

explain.body: Words, tone and body language arrive together, and the receiver can respond straight away. Misunderstandings are spotted from a puzzled face and cleared up immediately, before they become mistakes.

test.q: What allows misunderstandings to be cleared up quickly in a face-to-face meeting?
options: A permanent record of the discussion
The low cost of holding the meeting
Immediate two-way feedback
Contributions made at any time
test.why: Both parties can question and respond on the spot, so confusion is resolved before anyone leaves.

whyNot.0: Face to face has no automatic record.
whyNot.1: Face to face is usually the costlier option.
whyNot.3: Contributing at any time (asynchronous working) is a virtual advantage.

explain.body: Being in the room shows respect and allows empathy. That builds trust and relationships, and makes face to face the best method for bad news, conflict, negotiation and anything complex or contentious.

explain.h: Topics that call for face to face
head: Topic
Why in person

test.q: A project manager must tell a team their site is closing. Why is face to face the better choice?
options: Empathy and reassurance can be shown
The news is automatically documented
Remote staff can join at no extra cost
Nobody will need to ask any questions
test.why: Sensitive news needs empathy, and the speaker can see and respond to people's reactions in person.

whyNot.1: Face to face does not document itself; a written follow-up is needed.
whyNot.2: Low-cost remote reach is a virtual advantage.
whyNot.3: Sensitive news creates questions; face to face is chosen precisely so they can be asked.

explain.body: Face to face is time-consuming and costly (travel, venues), hard to arrange across locations and time zones, leaves no automatic record, and can be dominated by a few voices. Good chairing and minutes reduce the last two.

items.label: travel, venues, time away from work
hard across sites and time zones

test.q: Which statement about face-to-face meetings is true?
options: They are the cheapest way to reach many people
They give fewer non-verbal cues than email
They remove the need for any written follow-up
They leave no record unless minutes are taken
test.why: Nothing is captured automatically in a meeting; minutes or a follow-up note create the record.

whyNot.0: Gathering many people in person is costly; virtual methods are cheaper for wide reach.
whyNot.1: Face to face gives far more non-verbal cues than email, which has none.
whyNot.2: A written follow-up is exactly what covers the lack of a record.
